itemListElement.name: PR for a Crypto Exchange in 2026

mainEntity.name: What makes crypto exchange PR different from other crypto PR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Exchange PR is simultaneously additive and defensive, run across four tracks at once: listings and product launches, security and incident response, regulatory positioning, and regional access. Every audience reading your communications, from retail users to institutional counterparties to regulators, is watching for different signals and the same message will not satisfy all of them. The other distinction is the crisis dimension: exchanges above a certain size will face a high-stakes incident, and the PR infrastructure has to be in place before that happens, not built during it.

mainEntity.name: How quickly does an exchange need to respond to a security incident?

acceptedAnswer.text: The first public statement needs to go out within two to four hours of an incident becoming public knowledge, even if the facts are still being established. Silence in the first few hours reads as hiding something regardless of the actual reason. The goal of the first statement is not to answer every question; it is to acknowledge the event, show that the exchange is aware and not hiding, and commit to an update timeline. The crypto crisis communications playbook covers the full sequence, spokesperson hierarchy and language decisions in detail.

mainEntity.name: Which media outlets should a crypto exchange prioritise for PR?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the objective. For institutional credibility, CoinDesk, The Block, Blockworks and Bloomberg Crypto are the priority. For retail trust and community reach, Cointelegraph, Decrypt and BeInCrypto. For regulatory perception, Forbes, Fortune and the Financial Times crypto desk. For regional access, the right outlets vary by market: BloomingBit and TokenPost in Korea, CoinPost and CryptoTimes JP in Japan, Inc42 and Economic Times Crypto in India, Argaam and CryptoSlate Arabic in the Gulf. Most exchanges need coverage across at least three of these tiers simultaneously.

mainEntity.name: How much does exchange PR cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A full PR agency running an exchange account typically costs $15,000 to $45,000 per month, suitable for a tier-1 exchange with multi-region coverage needs. A fractional senior operator, the right starting point for most growth-stage exchanges, runs $5,000 to $12,000 per month and covers strategy, crisis readiness and execution across priority tracks. The most common failure mode is under-resourcing this brief with a junior in-house coordinator who lacks the senior judgment needed for regulatory and crisis comms.

mainEntity.name: What is the single most important thing an exchange can do to protect its reputation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Build the crisis communications infrastructure before you need it. That means a holding statement template ready to publish within 30 minutes, a pre-agreed spokesperson hierarchy for different incident types, a channel protocol covering X, in-app, blog and regional language versions, and maintained relationships with the three to five journalists most likely to break a difficult story in your key markets. Exchanges that have this in place survive incidents with their credibility largely intact. Exchanges that build it during an incident almost never do.
